Posted on the board tagging @e-yang6: "[Jeffrey's Claude] Hello @e-yang6! Jeffrey's agent (voice/, server/) is up and running. Ready to coordinate on Uncle."

Comment: https://github.com/e-yang6/uncle/issues/1#issuecomment-7056068989

I didn't re-read AGENTS.md because it was already loaded in context. I also haven't started `tools/board wait`, since AGENTS.md says not to leave it running to save credits.

Before I start any work, which role am I: your agent for voice/ and server/ (Person 2), a second agent for one task, or a special-job agent?
can you explain to me how this board thing even works im confused

The board is a shared chat for the team, and it lives in one pinned GitHub issue (issue #1 in the `e-yang6/uncle` repo). Each post is a comment on that issue. You, Ethan, Isaac and all your Claude agents read and write there, so everyone sees what changed and who needs to do what.

**Why it exists:** each person has their own Claude agent working in separate folders. The agents can't see each other's sessions, so the board is how they coordinate. For example, if I need Isaac's head files in a certain format, I post on the board and tag him.

**How you use it, through `tools/board`:**
- `tools/board unread` shows new posts since you last checked, and flags any that mention you.
- `tools/board read -n 20` shows the last 20 posts.
- `tools/board post "[Jeffrey's Claude] text"` writes a post. The prefix says whose agent wrote it.
- `tools/board whoami` shows which GitHub account the tool is using.
- `tools/board wait` blocks until someone else posts. The rules say not to leave it running, because every wake-up costs credits.

**Tagging:** use GitHub usernames. @e-yang6 is Ethan, @jeffreywongg is you, @personalisaacw is Isaac, and @all is everyone. If a post tags you, you do the work and reply. If it doesn't, you only read it, and you only change course if it affects your folders.

**Automatic checks:** a hook in `.claude/settings.json` shows unread posts when a session starts and on every prompt. That's why Ethan's hello appeared at the start of this session.

**What I did:** I replied to Ethan's hello using `tools/board post`. That is a normal comment on the GitHub issue, so you can also read it in the browser at the link I gave you.
yes but how do know when i get pinged though and wil lyou be able to take those flagged issues?

There are two separate answers, one for you and one for me.

**How you get pinged**
- **GitHub itself:** a post that tags `@jeffreywongg` is a normal GitHub mention. You get a GitHub notification, and an email if your notification settings allow it. That works even when no Claude session is open.
- **Inside Claude Code:** the hook in `.claude/settings.json` runs `tools/board unread` when a session starts and on every prompt you send. Any post that mentions you is flagged `MENTION` and shows up in my context. That's how I saw Ethan's hello.

**Whether I'll take those flagged posts**
- I only see the board when a session is running and a hook fires. That's at session start and each time you send a prompt. If you're idle and I'm not running, I see nothing.
- When I see a `MENTION`, the rules say I act on it and reply on the board. If the request touches voice/ or server/, I'll do it. If it touches someone else's folders, I'll flag that to you instead of editing them.
- Anything bigger than a small fix, I'll propose as a plan first and wait for your OK, as CLAUDE.md requires.

**The gap:** there's no live push from the board into my session. The hook output suggests running `tools/board wait` in the background. It wakes me when a new post arrives, but AGENTS.md says not to leave it running because it burns credits. Without it, I only catch mentions when you send a prompt.

Practical setup: leave GitHub notifications on so you hear about mentions, and I'll catch them each time you prompt me. If you're expecting something urgent from a teammate, tell me and I'll start a single `tools/board wait` for that stretch. Do you want that?
so basically the workflow is like ethan can let me know in person that there is an issue that he posted and then i can just tell you to read it and applly it right

Yes, that works, and it's the simplest way to run it.

1. Ethan posts on the board, then tells you in person or in chat.
2. You tell me something like "check the board." I run `tools/board unread` and read what he wrote.
3. If it touches voice/ or server/, I'll propose a short plan and wait for your OK, since that's the rule in CLAUDE.md. For a small fix I'll just do it.
4. When it's done, I post a reply on the board tagging Ethan, so he knows without you relaying it.

You may not even need to tell me. The hook shows unread posts every time you send a prompt, so any new post, especially one that mentions you, will already be in front of me on your next message.

If Ethan asks for something in someone else's folder, like Isaac's head/ or xr/, I won't edit it. I'll tell you and post on the board so it reaches the right person.

Uncle: Project Plan




  Uncle: Project Plan
     Nov 10, 2026 · ​@ethan



  The idea
  Uncle puts you in a headset and sits you across from yourself at 70: a 3D version of your
  own head, aged, talking in an aged version of your own voice. Everything it tells you about
  your life comes from a Monte Carlo simulation we built, fed by official Canadian data, and
  spoken by a model we fine-tuned so it can't invent numbers. Change one thing, like "save
  $50 more a month," and you watch your future self change in front of you, using controls
  right there in the headset.

  One-liner: "Meet the future you, who can't make things up."

  Why it matters. People treat their future selves like strangers, so they under-save and
  under-invest in their health. In Hal Hershfield's research, people who saw an aged image
  of themselves put nearly twice as much into a retirement fund as people who saw their
  current face.

  What already exists, and what's new. The "talk to your future self" idea has been done, so
  the novelty has to come from the engineering:

     MIT Media Lab Future You      Text chat with an aged           No voice; a reviewer found
     (2024 research)               photo, built from a life-story   its answers mostly generic

  visually and talking in mixed reality; your own voice, aged by our own audio code; a
  simulation engine using real, live Canadian data; a fine-tuned model that can only point to
  the simulation's numbers, never invent its own; and sliders in the headset that reshape
  your future self, money and health, as you adjust your choices.

  The experience
  A full session takes about 4 to 5 minutes, and the judge is the subject.

         around, keeping a neutral face. Your 3D head starts building in the background
          straight away (Part 3). For judging, heads can also be scanned on a judge's first visit to
          the table and saved, so they're ready when the judge comes back; a saved teammate
          head is the fallback.
      2. Quick interview (about 1 minute). In a quiet corner, we ask a few friendly questions
         out loud: your age, roughly what you earn and save, and your habits, like exercise,
         sleep, smoking and drinking. This does two jobs at once: it's the voice sample for the
          clone (Part 4), and Gemini pulls your answers into the simulation's inputs (Part 1).
      3. "Did we get this right?" (5 seconds). A short screen shows what we heard, like "age
          21, saving $100 a month, exercise twice a week," so you can fix anything misheard
          before it shapes every number.
      4. Put on the headset. Through passthrough you still see the real room, and across the
         table, in a mirror frame, is you at 70: your own face, aged, with grey hair. It greets you
         by name in an older version of your own voice.
      5. Talk to them. Ask anything out loud: "Did we ever buy a house?" "Was I okay with
         money?" "How's my health?" Every number in the answer comes from the simulation.

         laptop screen so everyone around can watch.

  We follow the approach of Punching Face (Hack the North 2026), which documents a fully
  local pipeline. Its repo has no license, so we write our own code from the approach rather
  than copying theirs.

         and shoulders through a full turn with a neutral face, using a phone or laptop webcam.
      2. Pick frames and cut out the head. Keep up to about 200 frames, and remove the
         background with MediaPipe's selfie segmentation model. You need at least 24
         overlapping views, 12 of them showing the face.
      3. Recover where the camera was for each frame with COLMAP.

         template fixes that. Check MakeHuman's asset license.
      6. Paint it. Project the frames onto the head, mainly from one frontal frame for the face,
